opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a really important first step, but it's definitely a work in progress. When we were putting together the code of ethics, a big part of the discussion was about what we can realistically ask researchers to report without making it feel like a bureaucratic checkbox exercise. Things like the potential negative societal impacts of the work, how the data was collected, whether there was consent, whether there are licensing issues, and also things like the compute used and, to some extent, the environmental footprint.

What I like about it is that it shifts the norm. For a long time, the attitude in our field was, "I'm just building the algorithm, what people do with it isn't my problem." And having it written into the submission process at a major venue like NeurIPS sends the signal that, no, actually, thinking about these things is part of doing good science.

That said, there are real limitations. A lot of researchers, especially more junior ones, don't necessarily have the training to anticipate the societal impacts of their work, so sometimes you get these very generic statements, like "this could be misused," which don't really help anyone. And there's the question of enforcement. Reviewers aren't always equipped to assess the ethics section either, which is why there's the ethics review process, but that doesn't scale to every paper, so it's mostly for flagged submissions.

On the compute and carbon side, which is close to my heart, I'd love for reporting to become more standardized. Right now people report things in very different ways, if at all, so it's hard to compare or to see trends across the field. Tools exist now to estimate energy use and emissions fairly easily, so the barrier is more cultural than technical at this point.

So overall I'd say it's a good foundation, and it's started conversations that weren't happening before. But I'd like to see it evolve with more guidance and examples for authors, more consistency in what's reported, and ideally some way to follow up on whether these reflections actually change how people do research rather than just becoming another box to tick.

r001.rationale: The candidate says researchers report compute and carbon information inconsistently, “if at all,” and identifies the barrier as cultural, communicating that missing reporting is a practical obstacle.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's important to say first that the code of ethics was really a community effort, and the reporting requirements, or what we ended up calling the checklist, grew out of a few years of iteration. The first version in 2021 was a bit more open-ended, kind of "please think about the broader impacts of your work," and what we saw was that people either wrote a paragraph of boilerplate or they skipped it entirely. So the move toward more structured questions was a response to that.

How do I assess it? I'd say it's a mixed bag, honestly. On the positive side, I think it's genuinely shifted norms. Five or six years ago, if you asked a machine learning researcher about the energy footprint of their training runs, or where their dataset came from and whether the people in it consented, a lot of them would look at you like you were asking something weird. Now those questions are on a form that every single submitting author has to look at. Even if they answer "not applicable," they've had to engage with the question, and I think that repeated exposure matters. Compute reporting in particular is something I care a lot about, and it went from basically nobody reporting it to a meaningful fraction of papers including at least GPU hours or hardware type.

The weaker side is enforcement and depth. A checklist is only as good as the reviewing around it, and reviewers are overloaded. They have, what, six papers, a couple weeks, and they're mostly focused on whether the method is sound and the results are real. The ethics section is often the last thing they look at, if they look at it at all. So you get a lot of "yes" boxes checked with very thin justification behind them. There's also the question of what happens when someone flags a real issue. We built an ethics review process, which I think is good, but it's a small number of reviewers handling cases that are often really nuanced, and the outcomes aren't always visible to the community, so it's hard to learn from them.

The other thing I'd flag is that reporting isn't the same as accountability. You can report that you trained on a scraped web corpus with no consent mechanism, and that's better than hiding it, but the paper still gets published. We've essentially chosen transparency over gatekeeping, and I think that's probably the right call for a research venue, but we shouldn't pretend transparency alone changes behavior. It gives people like me the data to then push on the issue, which is valuable, but the pushing still has to happen.

So if I had to sum it up, I'd say the reporting requirements have been successful at making certain considerations legible and normal, and less successful at making them consequential. And I think the next step isn't adding more boxes, it's figuring out how to make what's in those boxes actually feed back into decisions, whether that's reviewing, funding, or what gets highlighted at the conference itself.

r001.rationale: The response says authors previously skipped the ethics section or submitted boilerplate, and that compute reporting was rare. These are practical examples of researchers failing to record requested information.

astra-6.text:
I think reporting requirements are a useful starting point, but a requirement to report something isn’t the same as a requirement to address it. You can ask researchers to discuss the potential negative impacts of their work, but that doesn’t necessarily mean those impacts will influence how they conduct the research.

The challenge is making that reflection meaningful rather than a box you check at submission time. Are we asking questions that researchers can actually answer? Are we giving them enough guidance? And what happens when they identify a risk? For me, the value is in getting people to consider those questions earlier, when they can still change their approach, rather than treating ethics as a paragraph you add after the work is done.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether researchers can answer the prompts and warns that reflection may become a checkbox, but it does not identify researchers failing to record the requested information as a practical barrier.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re a good starting point. Asking researchers to report things like the compute they used and the potential impacts of their work makes those questions part of the research process, rather than an afterthought. But reporting alone doesn’t necessarily change behavior. You also need clear guidance about what to report, tools that make it easy, and some consistency in how that information is assessed.

There’s also a balance to strike. You don’t want this to become a box-checking exercise or put a disproportionate burden on researchers with fewer resources. Ideally, it helps people understand the trade-offs they’re making and gives the community information we can actually use to improve our practices.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the need for tools and guidance, but does not identify researchers’ failure to record the requested information as a practical barrier.
